<reason>Both sides argued well, but A built the cleaner decision rule and stuck to it: the motion says "prioritize intra-African trade and manufacturing OVER" exporting to distant rich markets, so PRO must defend the deprioritization, not just more processing. A then converted B's own strong line — "the destination of the cargo is a detail; its content is the argument" — into a serious problem for B, since destination is precisely what the motion contests. A also turned B's model cases (Korea, Chile, Norway, Malaysia, Indonesia) back on B by noting each sold refined output to distant rich markets rather than to neighbours, and pressed the funding mechanism: import machinery, power stations and ports are bought with export dollars. A's pressure questions were the best in the debate, forcing B to name instruments; when B produced a graduated export levy plus the claim that no forex is lost, A landed a crisp dilemma (either the levy bites and shrinks the earner, or it doesn't bite and there is no priority). B's counter that the levy redirects revenue into refining is plausible but again lands on ground A already concedes, so it did not restore the specifically intra-African half of the motion. B's best work was real: value capture in cocoa, commodity volatility and debt fragility, the jobs arithmetic, the sharp reframe that comparative advantage is built not inherited, and the excellent point that regional demand need not be invented because Africa already imports rice, sugar and cloth. B's closing charge that CON "opposes nothing but drift" had bite, but overstated things since A had explicitly named what it opposed (levies, diverted corridors, external tariff walls). A also answered B's Q2 concretely (single-spec dollar volume abroad versus thin, fragmented, low-income regional demand), whereas B's answer on consumer costs leaned on assertion. A's Rebuttal 2 being clipped for length is a real execution cost, and A's concession on processing gives away part of the motion, which keeps this from being a wide win.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>A's exploitation of B's "destination of the cargo is a detail" concession, followed by the levy dilemma — a levy that changes behaviour costs export earnings, one that doesn't isn't a priority at all — which forced B's plan to collapse either into A's own position or into costly protection.</best_rebuttal>
